issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile, 'kids crying' is not impossible, but it is a relatively specific trigger that would usually be supported by memory or appraisal content involving civilians/children; here the memory and appraisal items do not provide that link, so this trigger is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' implies an enduring physical injury theme, but the rest of the selected items do not support a bodily injury-focused combat presentation: memory items emphasize fragmentation/unreality, triggers emphasize intrusion/power imbalance, and strategies emphasize avoidance/hypervigilance rather than injury management. This appraisal is insufficiently anchored in the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Mere Tuilagi is a 66-year-old Fijian-American woman, divorced, who works as a curriculum designer for a mid-sized educational nonprofit. She was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to her primary care physician that she had not been sleeping properly for years and had recently stopped attending her organisation's in-person staff meetings altogether. Her PCL-5 score of 49 places her well within the clinical range for PTSD, and her presentation reflects a long and largely unaddressed history rooted in a combat exposure she sustained decades ago while serving as a civilian medical liaison in a forward operating zone.

The event itself occurred during a coordinated attack on a field compound. Mere had been in a briefing room with a commanding officer when the compound came under fire. She had no authority, no weapon, and no clear role in what followed - she was told to stay, to move, to wait, by people whose orders contradicted one another, and she complied because she had no choice. The sounds of rotor blades and aircraft filled the air throughout, first as the sound of potential rescue and then as something more ambiguous and terrifying when a helicopter passed low and the firing intensified. At one point she was physically moved by a soldier who grabbed her arm and directed her behind a wall without explanation. She survived. Several others did not. What she remembers of the aftermath is not a coherent sequence but a series of disconnected impressions - the colour of dust on a boot, the particular silence after the last shot, a face she cannot place - fragments that do not assemble into a story she can tell. She has said to her therapist that the memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to her, and when she tries to describe it, the words simply do not come. She knows what occurred, but the language for it seems to belong to someone else.

In the years since, these fragmented, wordless memories have not remained contained. They surface suddenly and without invitation - while Mere is reviewing curriculum materials, while she is eating lunch at her desk - and when they do, they arrive not as narrative recollection but as sensation and image, pulling her back into the compound with a vividness that makes the present feel thin. The sound of a helicopter is particularly destabilising. Working near an urban flight corridor, she hears rotors several times a week, and each time the sound reaches her, the fragments reassemble into something urgent and uncontrolled, flooding her with the same helplessness she felt that day. These triggered intrusions have, over time, deepened her conviction that she cannot trust herself to respond adequately - that in a moment of real danger, she would again be someone without agency, without the right words, without the capacity to act correctly. Being in any situation where another person holds authority over her reactivates this same fear, and she has come to dread team meetings, performance reviews, and any professional interaction in which her role is subordinate.

What Mere had come to believe, increasingly, was that she had to be on guard at all times, that she was fundamentally set apart from people around her who had not seen what she had seen, and that this separateness was permanent. These appraisals drove the strategies that now organise her daily life. She avoids going out beyond what her work requires, and when she must attend in-person events, she positions herself near exits - a habit so automatic she does not always notice she is doing it. She has also learned to suppress any strong emotion as it arises, treating feeling itself as a threat to her composure and safety. The consequence of these strategies has been substantial: by staying home, by cutting off her emotional responses, by withdrawing from professional gatherings, she has prevented the natural processing of what happened. The memories remain fragmented and unintegrated, and because they cannot be worked through, they continue to surface intrusively, confirming her sense of danger and perpetuating the vigilance and isolation she has tried to use as protection. Her avoidance has also cost her professionally - she was recently passed over for a project lead role, her manager noting her absence from collaborative spaces - and this loss has reinforced her belief that she is fundamentally different from others, someone who cannot be relied upon.

What finally brought Mere to seek help was a morning when a helicopter passed over her apartment building and she found herself on the floor of her kitchen, unable to stand for several minutes. She is most afraid that nothing can change at this point in her life. What she hopes, tentatively, is that someone might help her find the words.
